title: Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Rediscover the wonder of Christmas by focusing on God’s faithfulness and the hope found in Jesus.   The post  Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
summary_zh: 通过关注神的信实和耶稣的盼望，重新发现圣诞节的奇迹。“在圣诞节疲惫中寻找奇迹”一文首次出现在威克里夫。
title_zh: 在圣诞节疲惫中寻找奇迹
content: Christmas is supposed to be a season of wonder. Twinkling lights, familiar songs, meaningful traditions and time with people you love can all point toward the joy of celebrating Jesus’ birth. But when your December calendar fills with responsibilities and expectations, weariness can settle in before you realize it. Maybe you remember a time when Christmas felt different. As a child, you may have counted down the days and experienced joy in even the smallest traditions. As an adult, you might find yourself simply trying to catch your breath as you move from one responsibility to the next. In the middle of trying to make Christmas special for everyone else, it can be easy to miss the wonder yourself. But the Christmas story gives you an opportunity to slow down and remember what this season is really about. In Luke 1, before the story of Jesus’ birth begins, you meet people who knew what it meant to wait, wonder and trust that God was at work even when they couldn’t yet see what He was doing. Weary of Waiting Luke’s account of the life of Jesus doesn’t begin with Jesus’ birth; it begins instead with the story of Zechariah, an elderly priest who was tired of waiting. Zechariah had heard promises of Israel’s rescue from oppression and sin his entire life. That future must have seemed out of reach under Rome’s harsh control. But Zechariah and his wife, Elizabeth, also had an unfulfilled personal longing: “They had no children because Elizabeth was unable to conceive, and they were both very old” ( Luke 1:7, NLT ). One day, as Zechariah performed his duties in the temple, he was chosen to burn incense in the sanctuary — a rare honor with an unexpected result: While Zechariah was in the sanctuary, an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing to the right of the incense altar. Zechariah was shaken and overwhelmed with fear when he saw him. But the angel said, “Don’t be afraid, Zechariah! God has heard your prayer. Your wife, Elizabeth, will give you a son, and you are to name him John. You will have great joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great in the eyes of the Lord. He must never touch wine or other alcoholic drinks. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even before his birth. And he will turn many Israelites to the Lord their God. He will be a man with the spirit and power of Elijah. He will prepare the people for the coming of the Lord. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and he will cause those who are rebellious to accept the wisdom of the godly” ( Luke 1:11-17, NLT ). Trusting God in the Waiting An angel of the Lord appeared to Zechariah and announced that God had heard his prayer. Elizabeth would have a son named John who would “… prepare the people for the coming of the Lord” ( Luke 1:17b, NLT ). After years of waiting, God answered Zechariah and Elizabeth’s prayer as part of an even bigger story: They would finally have the child they had prayed for, and their son would prepare the way for Jesus. But Zechariah struggled to understand how it could possibly happen: “… ‘How can I be sure this will happen? I’m an old man now, and my wife is also well along in years’” ( Luke 1:18, NLT ). Zechariah could only see what seemed possible based on his circumstances. But God was asking him to trust what He had promised. The angel Gabriel responded by telling Zechariah that he would be unable to speak until the child was born, adding, “For my words will certainly be fulfilled at the proper time” ( Luke 1:20b, NLT ). Maybe you know what it’s like to pray about something for months or even years. It can be hard to keep trusting that God is working when it seems like nothing is changing. Zechariah’s story reminds us that even when we can’t see what God is doing, He is still faithful to His promises. Waiting is woven throughout the Christmas story. Maybe it’s part of your story too. 圣诞节应该是奇迹的季节 闪烁的灯光、熟悉的歌曲、有意义的传统和时间, 但当您12月的日历充满了责任和期望时,疲惫可以在您意识到之前安顿下来. 也许你记得圣诞节感觉不一样的时候

作为一个孩子,你可能已经 计数的日子和体验快乐 即使最小的传统。 作为一个成年人,你可能会发现自己只是 试图呼吸 当你从一个责任转移到下一个责任。 在试图让圣诞节对其他人特别的时候,自己也很容易错过奇迹.

但圣诞故事给了你一个机会,让你慢下来,并记住本季的真正内容. 在卢卡斯一世,耶稣诞生的故事开始前,你遇见了那些知道等待、好奇和相信上帝在工作的意义的人,即使他们还看不到他在做什么。 等待卢克对耶稣生活的描述,

以撒迦利亚的故事开始 撒迦利亚是一位老牧师 他厌倦了等待 撒迦利亚曾听到过以色列从压迫中解救出来的承诺,他一生都有罪。 罗马的严酷控制下,这一未来似乎已遥不可及。

但是,Zachariah和他的妻子Elizabeth也有未实现的个人愿望:“他们没有孩子,因为Elizabeth无法怀孕,而且他们都非常老”(Luke 1:7, NLT)。

一天,当撒迦利亚在圣殿中履行职责时,他被选中在圣殿烧香——这是罕见的荣誉,结果出乎意料:撒迦利亚在圣殿时,上帝的天使出现在他面前,站在香坛的右边. 撒迦利亚见到他时,被震撼和恐惧所压倒. 但天使说:"撒迦利亚,不要害怕!

他将是一个拥有以利亚精神和力量的人。 他会为主的到来为人民做准备. 他将把父亲们的心转向他们的孩子,他将使那些叛逆的人接受神的智慧”(Luke 1:11-17,NLT). 相信上帝在等待上帝的天使出现在撒迦利亚面前,并宣布上帝听到了他的祈祷.

Elizabeth将有一个名叫John的儿子,他将“为主的到来为人民做好准备”(Luke 1:17b, NLT)。 经过多年的等待,上帝回答了撒迦利亚和伊丽莎白的祈祷,作为更大的故事的一部分: 他们最终会有他们祈祷的孩子,他们的儿子会为耶稣准备道路.

但撒迦利亚却挣扎着去理解这怎么可能发生:“......我怎么能肯定这会发生呢? 我已是老人, Zachariah只能从他的情况看出什么是可能的。 但上帝要求他相信他所承诺的

天使Gabriel在回答时告诉Zachariah, 在孩子出生之前, 他无法说话, 并补充说, “我的话一定会在适当的时候实现”(Luke 1:20b, NLT)。 也许你知道祈祷几个月甚至几年是什么感觉。 很难继续相信上帝在工作 似乎没什么变化

撒迦利亚的故事提醒我们,即使我们看不到上帝在做什么,他仍然忠实于他的诺言。 等待被编织 整个圣诞节的故事。 也许这也是你的故事的一部分。 我们的四周免费的礼拜,“期待在等待中”,可以帮助你在《圣经》中度过时间。

title: No Incomplete Stories: God’s Word for All People
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: See how Bible translation helps communities access more of God’s Word through print, audio and sign language Scripture today.   The post  No Incomplete Stories: God’s Word for All People  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
summary_zh: 了解圣经翻译如何帮助社区通过印刷、音频和手语圣经获得更多上帝的话语。《No Incomplete Stories: God's Word for All People》一文首先出现在《Wycliffe》上。
title_zh: 没有不完整的故事：上帝给所有人的话语
content: Imagine reading a book, watching a show or listening to a podcast when suddenly the story just stops mid-sentence. Maybe the previous reader has ripped out a page, the series was canceled before the showrunners could wrap up the plotline, or the producer distributed the episode before realizing it was incomplete. How incredibly frustrating to not experience the full story from start to finish! It can leave us emotionally unsettled, frustrated or even distraught, because at our core, we desire completion. We want to know how things start and how they end. We don’t just want a taste, because it feels like a tease. We’re left wanting more . And we’re not alone in that desire! The same is true for communities around the world who are still waiting for the full counsel of God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. For some, they’re still waiting for the first verse of Scripture to be translated into their language. Others might have a few verses, chapters or Scripture portions . Still others are blessed with a complete New Testament but are waiting for the Old Testament so they can understand everything from Genesis to Revelation. They get a teaser of God’s great story — perhaps enough to understand who Jesus is and that He died for them — but they don’t have the full context as to why His sacrifice was so significant. The Bible changes everything, and together with our partners, Wycliffe believes that everyone should have access to the whole of Scripture. But don’t just take our word for it! Explore these Bible translation stories from our friends around the world who have personally experienced individual and community transformation as a result of encountering God through His Word. Want a glimpse of what it’s like to only have a portion of God’s Word? This “H ly B bl: Incomplete Scriptures” digital booklet helps you see what it’s like to have gaps in your understanding of the Bible. Explore the booklet → The Full “Outfit” of God’s Word Caroline always had access to a Bible growing up. But watching the Chonyi people of Kenya receive the New Testament in their language refreshed her passion for Bible translation, a mission she’s actively engaged in through SIL Kenya, a partner of Wycliffe. “They took a couple of Bibles, wrapped them up like a child,” she shared. “And there was a woman who was carrying the [Bibles]. And they were swinging and dancing, lifting up the [Bibles] and saying, ‘This is our child.’ Calling people, ‘Come,” in the Chonyi language. ‘Come and celebrate the child that has been born in us.’ “That is how the Chonyi people have taken the Bible — the New Testament — in their own language. That it is their child and they’re taking it seriously, making it bear fruit.” People gathered to hear Scripture read in their language, Bible studies began and the impact spread: 300 adults and 50 children gave their lives to Christ! At the celebration, the local pastors shared that now that the New Testament is complete, it’s like they have a shirt. But a shirt isn’t enough; they want a pair of pants (the Old Testament) to complete the outfit! Now work is underway to translate the Old Testament into Chonyi so that they can have the full “outfit” of God’s Word. Praise God! Watch how the Chonyi community celebrated the dedication of the New Testament in their community! One day, someone from the community called the local translation office with a request. “We have been enjoying this Jesus story from this elderly woman, and now it has broken. 想象一下看书,看秀或听播客,当故事突然停止中刑时. 可能之前的读者已经撕掉了一页,系列在放映者可以完成插图之前就被取消,或者制作者在意识到该集不完整之前就散发了该集. 无法从头到尾体验完整的故事 真是令人沮丧

它可能使我们情绪不安、沮丧甚至不安,因为我们的核心是希望完成。 我们想知道事情的开始和结束。 我们不只是想要品尝, 我们想要更多。 我们并非孤立于此,

世界各地的社区也是如此,他们仍在等待以他们明确理解的语言和形式充分听取上帝的话语。 他们仍在等待将第一部圣经翻译成自己的语言。 其他人可能有一些诗、章节或圣经部分。

还有一些人受到完整的"新约"的祝福,但正在等待"旧约",以便他们能够理解从创世纪到启示的一切. 他们得到了上帝伟大故事的嘲讽者 — — 或许足以理解耶稣是谁,而且他为他们而死 — — 但他们并没有完全了解为什么他的牺牲如此重要。

圣经改变了一切,与我们的伙伴们一起,威克利夫认为每个人都应该能够接触到整个圣经. 但不要只听我们的话! 探索这些来自我们世界各地朋友的圣经翻译故事,这些朋友通过"上帝之言"与上帝相遇,亲自体验过个人和社区的转变.

The post  When God’s Word Becomes Personal  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
summary_zh: 今天，在Faithly播客上， Alicia Lee欢迎Wycliffe Bible Translators USA内容营销高级总监Melissa Paredes就圣经翻译、母性以及圣经改变生活的力量进行有意义的对话。当上帝的话语成为个人时，这篇文章首先出现在威克里夫。
title_zh: 当神的话变成个人的
content: How old were you when you first learned that Jesus loves you? Perhaps you’ve always known it and can’t remember a day when you didn’t know the song “Jesus Loves Me” or couldn’t recite John 3:16 by heart. Maybe you were a teenager and learned about Jesus’ love through a friend or church summer camp. Or were in college and went to a concert where the gospel was clearly articulated. Maybe you were in the trenches of the workforce, and a coworker boldly shared with you about the God who radically changed their life. Regardless of how old you were, each of us who has chosen to follow Jesus has an origin story — a moment in our lives when the knowledge that “Jesus loves me, this I know, for the Bible tells me so” moved from head knowledge to heart belief. And from then on, our lives were transformed forever. This is the truth of the gospel and the power of understanding that Jesus loves you. People around the world are discovering the personal truth of John 3:16 for themselves in a language and format they clearly understand. Explore why understanding that “God so loved the world” transforms entire communities → A Changing Reality Throughout Christian history, the gospel has spread from one community to the next. Stories were told and retold, Scripture was translated, churches were planted, and discipleship deepened as people learned more about Jesus. Bible translation is foundational to all ministries of the church. It fuels evangelism, church planting, discipleship and more. It equips people to move from a blurry picture of who God is to a clear understanding and personal encounter with Jesus as Lord. Through Scripture, people are able to read, hear or see the love of God on display. Just two decades ago, most of the world’s language communities still needed Bible translation work to begin , let alone be completed. But praise God, in the last few years, we’ve seen tremendous progress made, with Bible translation underway in more languages than ever before . While the change in numbers is exciting, what’s more important is what they signify: Every number represents a person who has a story that matters to God. For these communities, the stories of future generations are being completely rewritten as children will now grow up never remembering a day when they didn’t have access to God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. That statement bears repeating: There will now be people who never remember a day when they didn’t have access to God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. From the first word of Genesis to the last word of Revelation, the Bible tells one incredible story: God’s love for the world and His invitation for people from every nation and language to know Him. Get a glimpse of how God continues writing this story today as more and more people are experiencing the power of His Word. Watch the video → A New Generation Growing Up With God’s Word Let’s take a look at some of the recent communities that are experiencing not only life transformation but generational transformation as they encounter Jesus personally through Scripture. Jakalteko | Guatemala The Jakalteko Bible was dedicated in July 2026 in Guatemala! During the celebration, John 1:1-18 was read aloud — a passage that focuses on Christ, the eternal Word and our Redeemer. Early on, many women in the community memorized Job 19 . Like Job, they had faced various hardships in their lives and identified with his suffering. The book reminded them that God remains in control and that, in the midst of difficult circumstances, their Redeemer will deliver them and comfort them in their pain. Today, they have the full counsel of God’s Word and can now see this Redeemer fulfilled in Jesus in the New Testament. They are overjoyed that the Bible has arrived in the language they were born into! When the Bible was distributed, one mother who is raising her family alone said with joy and tears: “Thank God we have the Bible in our language. Now

title_zh: 值得铭记的波兰感恩节
content: In 2018, God provided food for more than 70 people, double the expected number, at a Thanksgiving celebration Cal and Erin Hiebsch helped to host in order to share the gospel by telling the story of God’s provision for the Pilgrims on the first Thanksgiving. IMB Photo For Cal and Erin Hiebsch and their family, Thanksgiving is more than a cherished American holiday. Living and serving in Poland as International Mission Board missionaries, it has become one of their most effective opportunities to build relationships, share their culture and ultimately point people to Christ. While Poland celebrates Christmas and Easter on a grand scale, Thanksgiving is uniquely American. Many Poles are familiar with the holiday and curious about its traditions. Over the years, the Hiebsch family has learned to use that curiosity as a bridge for ministry. “Thanksgiving is probably one of our bigger entrées into American culture,” Cal explained. Each year, they invite friends, neighbors and participants from their English conversation clubs to experience a traditional Thanksgiving meal. For many guests, this is their first encounter with foods such as stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potato casserole and roasted turkey. Even finding a whole turkey in Poland can be a challenge, since stores more commonly sell turkey breasts and other cuts rather than the whole bird. One Thanksgiving, in particular, is especially memorable for the family. With the help of volunteers, Erin and the culinary crew carefully planned a special celebration. “We had people in four or five different kitchens across the city cooking,” she said. A generous spread of traditional American dishes filled the tables, and invitations had been extended throughout their community. Based on past events, they expected 20 to 30 people to attend. Erin said they planned for “double batches” of each dish with the intention of everybody trying a little of everything that was served. Servers fill up plates as IMB missionaries Cal and Erin Hiebsch and their friends host a Thanksgiving meal in Poland. They planned for 20 or 30 people to show up, but nearly 70 people filled the house. Thankfully, everyone had a full meal and heard the gospel message. IMB Photo As the evening began, guests kept arriving. More came through the doors. Then more. Soon the room was packed. Instead of the anticipated crowd of a few dozen, nearly 70 people showed up. The gathering became standing-room only. “I quietly asked a couple of the volunteer ladies to be praying that there would be enough for everyone,” Erin recalled. Cal was serving as emcee for the event, welcoming guests and sharing the Thanksgiving story. Meanwhile, others were distributing plate after plate of food. Every time someone entered the room, the challenge seemed to grow. How could the food possibly stretch far enough? Yet somehow, it did. People continued to receive full plates. Everyone ate. Conversations flourished around the tables. “The pumpkin pie was especially popular,” Erin said. Guests learned about the history of Thanksgiving and heard how God had provided for the Pilgrims during difficult circumstances. Most importantly, they heard the gospel woven naturally into the evening’s program. When the event finally concluded, the team compared notes and realized an astonishing experience occurred. “We doubled our crowd and had enough food for everyone to have a good Thanksgiving feast,” Cal recalled. To this day, Cal and Erin still talk about that evening. The experience remains difficult to explain, outside of God’s provision. They prepared for one number of guests and served more than twice as many. Whether miraculous or simply an extraordinary provision, the outcome was undeniable. More people than expected were welcomed, fed and exposed to the hope of Christ. An American holiday became a platform for meaningful conversations and gospel witness in a place far from home. content_zh:
2018年,上帝在感恩节庆祝活动Cal和Erin Hiebsch为70多人提供食物,是预期人数的两倍,他们通过讲述上帝在第一个感恩节上为朝圣者提供食物的故事,帮助分享福音. IMB Photo for Cal and Erin Hiebsch and their family, 感恩节不仅仅是一个珍视的美国节日.

在波兰生活和担任国际传教委员会传教士,已经成为他们建立关系、分享其文化并最终指向基督的最有效机会之一。 虽然波兰在大尺度上庆祝圣诞节和复活节,但感恩节是独特的美国人. 许多波兰人对节日很熟悉,对其传统很好奇.

多年来,Hiebsch家族学会了利用这种好奇心作为部委的桥梁。 Cal解释道, “感恩大概是我们美国文化中一个更大的参与者。 每年,他们都会邀请他们英语对话俱乐部的朋友,邻居和参与者体验传统的感恩节餐.

对于许多嘉宾来说,这是他们第一次遇到填料,绿豆砂锅,甜薯砂锅和烤火鸡等食物. 即使是在波兰找到整只火鸡也可能是一个挑战,因为商店更常出售火鸡乳房和其他切口,而不是整只鸟. 特别是感恩节对家庭来说特别值得纪念。

在志愿者的帮助下,艾琳和烹饪船员精心策划了一场特别的庆祝活动. 她说:「我们有四五个不同的厨房, 美国传统菜肴的慷慨推广为餐桌填满了餐桌,在他们的社区内发出了邀请。 根据过去的事件,他们预计有20至30人参加。

Erin说,他们计划将每道菜“分两批”使用,目的是让每个人都尝试一下所服务的东西。 服务器在IMB传教士卡尔和艾琳·希布希及其朋友在波兰举办感恩节晚宴时填满了盘子. 他们计划有20到30人出现,但将近70人填满了房子.

谢天谢地,每个人都吃过一顿饭,听到了福音的信息. IMB 图片 随着夜晚的开始, 客人不断到达。 更多人从门进来了 再来 很快房间就收拾好了. 而不是预期的几十人的人群,近70人出现了. 聚会变成了只有站着的房间。

Erin回忆道, “我悄悄地要求几位女志愿者祈祷, 卡尔当时担任了该活动的代表,欢迎嘉宾并分享感恩节的故事. 与此同时,其他人在分发盘子后再分发食物。 每次有人进入房间,挑战似乎越来越大。 食物怎么够长?

然而,不知何故,它确实如此。 人们继续收到满板。 每个人都吃了。 围绕桌子的议论蓬勃发展. 艾琳说,“南瓜派特别受欢迎。” 嘉宾们了解感恩节的历史,并听说上帝在艰难的情况下为朝圣者提供了什么. 最重要的是,他们听到了晚间节目中自然编织的福音。

当活动最终结束时,团队比较了笔记,意识到发生了惊人的经历. Cal回忆道, “我们的人口增加了一倍, 直到今天,卡尔和艾琳仍在谈论那个晚上. 除了上帝的规定之外,这些经历仍然难以解释。

他们为1位客人做准备,服务人数为2倍以上. 无论是神奇的还是简单的特别的规定,结果都是不可否认的。 更多的人受到基督的欢迎、食物和希望。 一个美国节日成为了在远离家的地方进行有意义的交谈和福音见证的平台.

title_zh: 第一人称：我们为什么请您祷告
content: April Bunn, IMB director of global prayer strategies, shows messengers at an SBC annual meeting the latest Loving the Lost prayer resource. IMB Photo April Bunn directs global prayer strategies for the IMB. IMB Photo My husband and I moved from our home in Tennessee to South Asia when we were in our 20s. God called us to serve overseas through the International Mission Board, and we were excited to share the gospel with those who had not yet had an opportunity to hear it. As we began to plant our lives in a city on the other side of the world, we quickly realized the task before us was massive. We were surrounded by millions of people, the vast majority of whom were spiritually lost and on a trajectory to an eternity separated from Christ. We were grappling with a new language, a different culture, unfamiliar foods, homesickness and the list went on. We were overwhelmed. The reality of the lostness around us felt too much to carry. As we turned to God for help, He reminded us that we were not meant to carry this task alone. We had been sent as laborers to the nations, but the Great Commission was given to the whole Church. The Church was our partner in this work. As we began intentionally inviting brothers and sisters in the U.S. to walk with us regularly in prayer, we saw God move in unmistakable ways. They carried the burden of lostness with us, and they also rejoiced with us as we saw God work. We had been sent as laborers to the nations, but the Great Commission was given to the whole Church. The Church was our partner in this work. Today, after two decades in South Asia, I have the privilege of encouraging and equipping believers to pray for people and places around the world through my work with the IMB. In doing so, I’m continually reminded that God’s mission is His work, and we are utterly dependent on Him to accomplish it. Missionaries can faithfully go, learn languages, share the gospel and disciple believers, but they cannot change hearts. God can. That is why we ask you to pray. Prayer is strategic to the Great Commission, and e very believer can take part in it. As the Church, we are living between the giving of the Great Commission and its culmination in the great multitude we see in Revelation 7:9, where people from every nation, tribe, people and language will stand before the throne worshiping God together. Until that day, we go to take the good news to a world in need. And we pray, asking God to do what only He can do. Through prayer, every believer, regardless of age or location, can intercede for places we may never be able to go ourselves. No country or people group is closed to the work of the Spirit through the prayers of God’s people. We may not see every answer to those prayers in our lifetime; some will only become visible when we stand before the throne and see the faces of those God drew to Himself. Until then, we keep praying. April Bunn, IMB director of global prayer strategies, shows messengers at an SBC annual meeting the latest Loving the Lost prayer resource. The new Loving the Lost is available for free from the IMB. IMB Photo Paul tells us in Colossians 4:2 to “continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.” To be watchful means we are paying attention and expecting God to work. The Mixtec people of Mexico have reminded me what that kind of watchful, steadfast prayer looks like. Beginning in 2008, IMB missionaries serving among the Mixtec began sharing prayer requests with IMB’s prayer office so they could be shared widely and more believers could join them in prayer. The requests were simple. Pray for open hearts. Pray for opportunities to share Bible stories in the Mixtec language. Pray for people to help make Scripture accessible. Pray for God to open doors. Month after month and year after year, people prayed for access to villages, for the first believers, for courage in the face of persecution. Today there is a growing fellowship of Mixtec believers. content: An IMB missionary among the Deaf records a Bible story in sign language. IMB Photo Every dollar you give to the Lottie Moon offering goes to support missionaries like Noah Lewis who live and serve among the lost. Will you consider giving today? Noah Lewis couldn’t help signing along with a worship song playing in the background as Deaf friends gathered in his home for dinner. The International Mission Board appoints missionaries who are both Deaf and hearing to serve among the global Deaf. Many missionaries learn sign language for the first time, while others use their American Sign Language to more quickly learn global sign languages. IMB Photo The International Mission Board missionary was sitting in the living room with his roommate and two friends while others prepared food nearby. As a young, single adult, simply opening the doors to his home in the Middle East has created some of his most fruitful opportunities for gospel conversations. That evening, Lewis was stirred to worship the Lord. “I just love worshiping in sign language because it’s a full-body experience,” Lewis said. Lewis, who is hearing, began signing the song in American Sign Language. Across the room, one of his Muslim friends watched intently. When the song ended, his friend told him it was beautiful and asked to see another. Lewis explained that Christians use songs to worship God. His friend compared what he had seen to hearing the Islamic call to prayer. The exchange opened an opportunity for Lewis to explain Christian worship and why Christians worship Jesus. When his friend asked to see more, Lewis continued signing songs from the playlist. “He was just really captivated by it,” Lewis said. “It really felt like in that moment the Spirit was working in his heart.” The conversation did not end with a profession of faith. Instead, it became another step in a friendship where Lewis has watched spiritual curiosity grow over time. During Ramadan, the same friend asked about fasting. On another night, he asked how Christians pray. Each question has allowed Lewis to explain what Christians believe and why he follows Jesus. Those conversations reflect much of Lewis’ ministry. He has served in the Middle East for nearly a year and a half, spending much of his time learning sign language and building relationships in the local Deaf community. Learning sign language, like learning any language, requires time, practice and immersion in the community that uses it. For Lewis, that process has looked different from the experience of missionaries who can spend several hours each day in a formal language school. There are no comparable sign language centers where he serves, so much of his language learning happens through relationships with Deaf friends. Although Lewis has not had a dedicated language tutor since arriving on the field, personal relationships help him develop a strong conversational understanding of the sign language used where he serves. The process has also drawn him more deeply into the Deaf community he came to reach. “I want to genuinely learn about their language,” he said. “I want to be friends with them. I want to know who they are.” As Lewis’ ability to communicate grows, relationships deepen and opportunities to share the gospel follow. Even when he doesn’t know the exact sign he needs, friends help him find ways to communicate biblical truths. Lewis has learned to faithfully use the language he has while continuing to grow in his ability to communicate the gospel clearly. An IMB worker among the Deaf records a Bible story. Generous giving to the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering supports missions among the global Deaf. Lewis currently lives and serves in the Middle East, but he arrived on the field with a long-term desire to serve in Central Asia. His recent trip allowed him to learn more about the culture, Deaf communities a
content_zh:
一名IMB在聋人中的传教士用手语记录圣经故事. IMB照片 你给洛蒂月球的每一美元 都用来支持传教士 比如诺亚·刘易斯 你会考虑今天给钱吗? 当聋人朋友聚集在家中吃饭时,

国际代表团委员会任命聋人和听力传教士在全球聋人中任职。 许多传教士首次学习手语,而其他传教士则使用他们的美国手语更快地学习全球手语.

IMB照片 国际传教委员会传教士与他的室友和两个朋友坐在客厅里,而其他人则在附近准备食物. 作为一个年轻、单身的成年人,只要打开通往他在中东的家的大门,就为他的福音对话创造了一些最富有成果的机会。 当晚,刘易斯被激起崇拜主.

「我只是喜欢手语崇拜, 正在听话的刘易斯开始用美国手语签署歌曲. 在房间里,他的一个穆斯林朋友故意观看。 歌曲结束的时候,他的朋友告诉他这很美丽,并请求见另一首. 刘易斯解释说,基督徒使用歌曲来崇拜上帝.

他的朋友比较了他所看到的听到的伊斯兰祈祷的呼声. 这次交流为刘易斯解释基督教崇拜和基督徒为何崇拜耶稣提供了机会. 当他的朋友要求看到更多时,刘易斯继续从播放列表上签名歌曲. 刘易斯说:“他只是被它迷住了。”

“在那个时刻,精神确实在他心中发挥作用。” 对话没有以信仰职业结束。 相反,它成为友谊的又一个步骤,刘易斯目睹了精神好奇心随时间推移而增长. 斋月期间,同友问斋事. 在另一个晚上,他问基督徒如何祈祷.

每个问题都让刘易斯解释基督徒相信什么,为什么他跟随耶稣. 这些谈话反映了刘易斯部的许多情况。 他在中东服务了近一年半,花了很多时间学习手语,在当地聋人社区建立关系.

学习手语,就像学习任何语言一样,需要时间,练习和沉浸在使用手语的社区中. 对刘易斯来说,这一进程与传教士的经历不同,传教士可以每天在一所正式语言学校中度过几个小时。

他所服务的手语中心并不存在类似的手语中心,所以他的许多语言学习都是通过与聋人朋友的关系发生的. 虽然刘易斯自到达球场后便没有专门的语言辅导员,但个人关系帮助他发展出对他所服务的手语的强烈的对话理解.

这一过程还使他更深入地融入了他所接触的聋人社区。 他说:“我想真正了解他们的语言。” “我想与他们成为朋友。 我想知道他们是谁。” 随着刘易斯沟通能力的增长,关系加深,分享福音的机会随之而来。

即使他不知道自己需要什么具体标志, 刘易斯学会了忠实使用他拥有的语言,同时继续增强他明确传达福音的能力. 一个IMB工人在聋人中记录了一个圣经故事. 慷慨地给洛蒂月亮圣诞节 提供全球聋人中的支持任务

IMB 图片 当计划消失时 在最近访问中亚期间,这种对上帝的依赖得到了更明确的关注。 刘易斯目前在中东生活和服役,但他远期带着在中亚服役的愿望赶到现场. 他最近的旅行使他能够更多地了解文化,聋人社区

summary: God continues to call His people to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth. summary_zh:
上帝继续召唤 他的族人将福音传到地底 11月9日,在俄亥俄州代顿附近的第一浸信会Kettling教堂的Sugarcreek校区,33名国际传教委员会传教士站在家人、朋友和支持者面前,申明他们服从这一呼吁。

独立浸信会的受托人任命了得到充分支持的传教士,他们代表10个州,包括俄亥俄州的两名候选人,以及许多致力于圣的南方浸信会教会。
title_zh: 俄亥俄州派遣庆祝活动确认33名IMB传教士为全球服务
content: Participants at the IMB Sending Celebration on Nov. 9, 2026, celebrated God's faithfulness in sending 33 new missionaries to the nations. Held at the Sugarcreek campus of First Baptist Kettering near Dayton, Ohio, the event launched the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio annual gathering. For security reasons, some newly appointed missionaries are not publicly identified. IMB Photo God continues to call His people to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth. During a Sending Celebration Nov. 9 at the Sugarcreek Campus of First Baptist Church Kettering, near Dayton, Ohio, 33 International Mission Board missionaries stood before family, friends and supporters, affirming their obedience to that call. Trustees of the IMB appointed the fully supported missionaries who represent 10 states – including two candidates from Ohio – and many Southern Baptist churches committed to sending and sustaining those called by God to go to the mission field. Senior Pastor Chad Keck welcomed those in attendance, sharing his appreciation for the partnership with Southern Baptist churches to cooperatively send and support missionaries. The Sending Celebration is meeting in conjunction with the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio. Chad Keck, senior pastor of First Baptist Kettering near Dayton, Ohio, left, and Jeremy Westbrook, executive director-treasurer of the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio, right, welcome guests gathered for the IMB Sending Celebration, which kicked off the convention’s annual gathering. IMB Photo Among those who shared their stories include a couple who answered an unexpected call later in life, a couple who are returning to Albania and to people they could not forget; and a couple who moved from welcoming the nations in Canada to going to Fiji. All of them shared their stories before the Sending Celebration. Unexpected invitation to go On Dec. 5, 2025, what seemed like an ordinary FaceTime call became a turning point for Rob Boss. As he spoke with his daughter, Hannah, during her IMB training, Rob sensed God speaking clearly to his heart: “You can do this too.” The impression was unexpected. After decades of writing, Christian education, seminary teaching and active support of missions, overseas service had never been part of Rob and Stephanie Boss’ plans. “It wasn’t an audible voice, but it was so clear,” Rob said. “It was Him. It was so kind and so gentle and so encouraging.” The moment drove him to his knees in surrender. When Stephanie came home later that day, he told her he believed God was calling them to the nations. Her response was immediate. “Thrilled is the right answer,” she said. The next day, the couple contacted the IMB and began the application process. Though missions had long been part of their family’s story, Rob and Stephanie Boss sensed God leading them to overseas service while encouraging their daughter, Hannah, during her missionary training. Sent by Wedgwood Baptist Church in Fort Worth, Texas, they are now headed to Colombia, where they will serve through theological education. IMB Photo Looking back, the Bosses see the Lord’s hand preparing them long before they realized where He was leading. “God brought us together in the summer of 1990 at Glorieta, New Mexico, where we met and married,” Stephanie said during the Sending Celebration. What followed was years of ministry, teaching, parenting and navigating life’s unexpected turns, which taught them to hold plans loosely and trust God completely. “We did not have a clue about what life held in front of us,” Stephanie said. “We just knew we wanted to follow the Lord.” Their calling also continues a family legacy. Rob’s mother served with the IMB in Africa after retirement, helping inspire Hannah’s service in South Korea. Now, three generations of the same family have answered God’s call to the nations. Rob and Stephanie expressed deep gratitude for their sending church, Wedgwood Baptist Church in Fort Worth, whose strong commitment to missions
content_zh:
2026年11月9日的IMB送信庆典的参与者,庆祝上帝向各国派遣33名新传教士的忠诚. 该活动在俄亥俄州代顿附近的第一浸信会Kettling的Sugarcreek校园举行,在俄亥俄州发起了浸信会州议会年会。 出于安全考虑,一些新任命的传教士没有公开身份.

IMB图片神继续呼叫 他的族人将福音传到地底 11月9日,在俄亥俄州代顿附近的第一浸信会Kettling教堂的Sugarcreek校区,33名国际传教委员会传教士站在家人、朋友和支持者面前,申明他们服从这一呼吁。

IMB的受托人任命了代表10个州的全力支持的传教士 — — 包括俄亥俄州的两名候选人 — — 以及许多南方浸信会教会承诺将那些被上帝召唤去传教的传教士送去并维持下去.

高级牧师Chad Keck欢迎与会者,与他一样感谢与美南浸信会教会合作派遣和支持传教士。 送教庆典会与俄亥俄州的浸信会州会议同时举行.

俄亥俄州代顿附近第一浸信会Ketting的资深牧师查德·凯克(Chad Keck)左翼,俄亥俄州浸信会执行董事兼创始人杰里米·韦斯特布鲁克(Jeremy Westbrook)右翼欢迎前来参加IMB送信庆典的来宾,这驱散了大会的年度集会。

在分享自己故事的人中,有一对夫妇在生活后期意外地接了电话,一对夫妇正在返回阿尔巴尼亚,一对夫妇无法忘记;一对夫妇从欢迎加拿大各国搬到斐济。 他们都分享了他们的故事 在送信庆典之前。 意外邀请 Dec 上。

5, 2025, 看起来像一个普通的FaceTime电话成为Rob Boss的转折点. 当他和他的女儿汉娜在IMB训练期间交谈时,罗布感应到上帝对他说的很清楚:“你也可以这样做。” 印象出乎意料。

经过几十年的写作、基督教教育、神学院教学和对使团的积极支持,海外服务从未成为罗布和斯蒂芬妮·博斯计划的一部分。 Rob说, “这不是一个声音, “这是他。 它是如此善良和温柔,如此鼓舞人心。” 那一刻,他被迫跪在地上投降。

当斯蒂芬妮当天晚些时候回家时,他告诉她,他相信上帝在召唤他们到各国. 她立即作出反应。 她说,“令人惊叹的是正确的答案。” 次日,夫妇联系IMB,开始了申请程序.

虽然传教团早就是他们家庭故事的一部分,但罗布和史蒂芬妮·博斯感知到,在传教团训练期间,他们带领他们到海外服务,同时鼓励他们的女儿汉娜。 由德克萨斯州沃思堡的韦奇伍德浸信会(Wedgwood Baptist Church)派遣,他们现在前往哥伦比亚,通过神学教育服务.

IMB照片回想起来,老板们看到主的手 在他们意识到在哪里之前很早就准备了 他是领导。 " 1990年夏天,上帝把我们带到了新墨西哥州格洛里埃塔,我们在那里相遇并结婚。 " Stephanie在送货庆典上说。

接下来是多年的教职、教职、养育和过着意想不到的转折,教他们松动计划,完全相信上帝。 Stephanie说:“我们不知道我们面前的生活是什么。” 我们只知道我们想跟随主。 他们的召唤也延续了家庭遗产。

罗布的母亲退休后在非洲为IMB效力,帮助激励汉娜在韩国服役. 现在,同一家庭的三代人响应了上帝向各国发出的呼吁。 Rob和Stephanie深表感谢他们派来的教会Worth堡的Wedgwood浸信会教堂,他们坚定致力于使命

对在塞内加尔服务的国际传教委员会传教士卡森·韦斯特来说,奥运会是一个独特的机会,不仅可以让游客接受福音,还可以动员当地教会在奥运会火焰熄灭很久后,在福音仪式中发挥更积极的作用。
title_zh: IMB传教士到位，准备鼓励塞内加尔教会开展青年奥运会外展活动
content: A Senegalese Christian shares the gospel with event volunteers during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. IMB Photo As athletes and spectators from around the world fill the streets of Senegal for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, missionaries and local believers are praying the event will leave behind more than medals and memories. For Carson West, an International Mission Board missionary serving in Senegal, the Games represent a unique opportunity not only to engage visitors with the gospel but also to mobilize local churches to take a more active role in evangelism long after the Olympic flame is extinguished. “This is the first Olympic event ever held on the continent of Africa,” West said. “For us, it was an opportunity to ask, ‘What are we going to do with this?’” The Youth Olympic Games, which began Oct. 31 and end Nov. 13, are taking place across three host cities: Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly. Event organizers expect nearly 2,700 athletes, ages 14-17, to participate in 35 sports and represent more than 200 delegations. The Games have drawn a million spectators, and West reported more than 6,000 event volunteers are staffing all the venues. With so many people gathering in Senegal, West and his team concentrated on preparing Senegalese churches for evangelistic opportunities. “We could run and hide, or we could do this thing,” West said, recalling an early conversation with teammates. “We decided we were going to do this thing.” The 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, is the first Olympic event held on the continent of Africa. IMB Photo West serves as team leader for IMB work in Senegal, where ministry efforts focus on three areas: gospel engagement, church advancement and community development. The Youth Olympic outreach naturally aligns with the first two priorities. “Our approach has been to mobilize the local church,” he said. “This is their backyard.” Instead of relying on a large influx of international volunteers, though there is one volunteer team from the United States serving, the strategy has centered on equipping local believers. Senegal has four Baptist churches in the greater Dakar area. Many leaders representing the congregations, as well as other ministry partners, participated in evangelism training designed specifically for the Games. Church leaders and ministry partners in Senegal participate in an evangelism training session specifically designed to share the gospel during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. IMB Photo A key outreach method involves trading commemorative pins, a familiar Olympic tradition. Volunteers use the exchange as a natural conversation starter before offering gospel-centered materials. Each pin is accompanied by a card featuring a QR code connected to a digital engagement platform adapted from previous Olympic and World Cup outreaches. Visitors who scan the code are directed to online resources and can connect with trained digital responders. Experienced volunteers in the U.S. are helping provide follow-up conversations. “We’re building on strategies that have been used effectively in previous Olympic Games,” West said. “It’s an easy, non-intimidating way to start gospel conversations.” Trading commemorative pins is an Olympic tradition. Volunteers use these pins to start gospel-driven conversations during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. Each pin is accompanied by a card featuring a QR code that connects people to trained digital responders. IMB Photo The effort extends beyond Dakar. IMB teams and church partners are positioned in each of the three host cities. An IMB team, which includes three global missionary partners, is helping coordinate outreach efforts in Diamniadio, and an IMB team along with a Baptist church is organizing efforts in Saly. West believes the greatest potential impact may be felt not among international visitors but among Senegalese believers themselves. Senegal is approximately 95% Muslim and 0.2% evangelical. content_zh:
一名塞内加尔基督徒在达喀尔青年奥林匹克运动会期间与活动志愿者分享福音. IMB 相片 当来自世界各地的运动员和观众为2026年达喀尔青年奥林匹克运动会而填满了塞内加尔的街道时,传教士和当地信徒正在祈祷这次活动将留下比奖牌和记忆更多的东西.

对在塞内加尔服务的国际传教委员会传教士卡森·韦斯特来说,奥运会是一个独特的机会,不仅可以让游客接受福音,而且可以动员当地教会在奥运会火焰被扑灭后很长一段时间里在传教中发挥更积极的作用。 “这是非洲大陆有史以来第一次举行的奥林匹克活动,”West说。

" 对于我们来说,这是一个机会,可以问:‘我们该怎么办? ' 从10月31日开始到11月13日结束的青年奥林匹克运动会正在三个主办城市举行:达喀尔、迪亚姆尼亚迪奥和萨利。 活动组织者预计有近2700名14至17岁的运动员参加35个运动会,并代表200多个代表团.

该运动会吸引了一百万观众,而西部报道有超过6000名活动志愿者为所有会场配备人员. 如此多的人聚集在塞内加尔,韦斯特和他的团队集中力量为塞内加尔的教会准备福音会的机会. West说:“我们可以跑去躲起来,或者做这件事。”

“我们决定这样做。” 2026年塞内加尔达喀尔青年奥林匹克运动会是非洲大陆首次举办的奥林匹克运动会. IMB Photo West是IMB在塞内加尔工作的团队领导,该部的工作集中在三个领域:福音参与、教会进步和社区发展。 青年奥林匹克运动会的外联自然符合前两个优先事项。

他说,“我们的做法是动员地方教会”。 这是他们的后院。 战略不是依赖大量国际志愿者的涌入,而是以装备当地信徒为中心,尽管有一个来自美国的志愿者团队在服役. 塞内加尔在大达喀尔地区有四所浸信会教堂。

许多代表会众的领导人以及其他部委伙伴参加了专门为奥运会设计的福音会培训。 塞内加尔的教会领袖和部委伙伴参加了一个福音会培训班,专门在达喀尔青年奥林匹克运动会期间分享福音。

IMB Photo A关键推广方法涉及交易纪念针,这是熟悉的奥林匹克传统. 志愿者在提供以福音为核心的材料之前,将交换作为自然对话的起步器. 每枚接针都附有一张卡片,上面有QR码,与从之前的奥运会和世界杯推广活动改编而来的数字接战平台相接.

扫描代码的访客被引导到在线资源中,可以与经过训练的数字响应器连接. 在美国有经验的志愿者正在帮助提供后续对话. 西方说, “我们正在借鉴以往奥运会有效运用的战略。

“开口福音对话是一个简单、非暗示性的方法。 交易纪念针是奥林匹克传统. 志愿者在达喀尔青年奥林匹克运动会期间利用这些针头开始福音驱动的对话. 每个接针都配有以QR代码为特色的卡片,将人与训练有素的数字响应器相接. IMB 相片 这项工作超越了达喀尔。

IMB团队和教会合作伙伴在三个东道城市各设一站. 一个由3个全球传教伙伴组成的一个IMB小组正在协助协调迪亚姆尼亚迪奥的外联工作,一个IMB小组和一个浸信会教会正在萨利组织努力。

西方认为,国际游客、塞内加尔信徒本身可能感受到最大的潜在影响。 塞内加尔穆斯林约占95%,福音派约占0.2%。 在一个269人死亡的国家d

title: IMB seeks teachers, healthcare workers, business professionals to serve as missionaries
summary: When most Southern Baptists think of missionaries, they often picture church planters and evangelists. But leaders with the International Mission Board say some of the greatest needs today are for professionals whose work happens behind the scenes. IMB leaders report that critical roles such as teachers, healthcare workers, counselors, accountants, logistics specialists and member care personnel are helping advance the Great Commission in ways many churches never see. Doreen Baker, IMB director
summary_zh: 当大多数"南方浸信会"想到传教士时,他们常常会描绘出教会的植树人和福音派. 但国际使命委员会的领导人说,今天最需要的是那些在幕后工作的专业人员。 咨监委领导人报告说,教师、保健工作者、顾问、会计师、后勤专家和成员护理人员等关键角色正在帮助推进大委员会,许多教会从未看到过。 多琳·贝克,IMB导演
title_zh: IMB寻求教师、医护人员、商业专业人士担任传教士
content: IMB missionary Dr. Heidi Haun, left, checks on patients at Baptist Medical Centre in Nalerigu, Ghana. There are needed roles for IMB missionaries in healthcare, ministering to the needs of local populations and utilizing this time to minister to spiritual needs. IMB Photo When most Southern Baptists think of missionaries, they often picture church planters and evangelists. But leaders with the International Mission Board say some of the greatest needs today are for professionals whose work happens behind the scenes. IMB leaders report that critical roles such as teachers, healthcare workers, counselors, accountants, logistics specialists and member care personnel are helping advance the Great Commission in ways many churches never see. Doreen Baker, IMB director of TCK (third culture kid or missionary kid) education, sees a constant need for education professionals. Teachers are needed in international schools, which cover a variety of global educational entities, and in other settings to provide for missionary kids and their educational needs. “Teachers are significant in that not only are they providing instruction for students, but they are an integral part of the core missionary task ,” Baker said. “We also have great needs for consultants to support our families on the field with their children’s education in many ways.” Baker previously served 25 years teaching in Asia and experienced how education creates access to missions where traditional pathways may be limited. IMB missionary Ellie Bohrer teaches a 12th grade World Views class at Black Forest Academy in Germany. The IMB is seeking other educators, like Bohrer, who are willing to use their skills on the mission field. IMB Photo Scott Ray, IMB senior director of global deployment, noted that many missionary positions go unfilled simply because they fall outside traditional perceptions of missionary service. He said professional skills can provide both practical ministry support and access to countries where traditional missionary visas are difficult to obtain. Opportunities exist for finance professionals, veterinarians, medical workers, Send Relief personnel and others. Healthcare remains one of the most strategic areas in demand. Tom Hicks, IMB director of global health strategies, said many medical professionals have the wrong perception about mission work. “We do have an issue where people will select out because they don’t think that what they do is useful on the mission field,” he said. In reality, Hicks said many areas across the globe are increasingly seeking family medicine physicians, internists, pediatricians, pediatric nurse practitioners, OB providers, physical therapists, occupational therapists, speech pathologists and lactation consultants. The need is especially significant in sub-Saharan Africa, where young populations create a growing demand for pediatric care. Healthcare professionals also provide a unique advantage in countries that restrict missionary activity. “Missionaries with a vocational value, like healthcare missionaries, have opportunities to go places that others can’t go,” Hicks said. Another often-overlooked ministry is member care, which focuses on the spiritual, emotional, mental and relational health of IMB missionaries. Chris Martin is the IMB director of global member care. “Member care missionaries stand alongside those missionaries that are thought of traditionally as church planters or evangelists and support them,” Martin said. Many who serve in these roles come from counseling backgrounds and help missionaries navigate stress, conflict, grief and other challenges that can affect long-term ministry effectiveness. Martin compares their role to Aaron and Hur in Exodus 19, holding up Moses’ arms during battle, strengthening those serving on the front lines. IMB missionary Glen Garner uses his business skills and experience as the logistics director for missionaries serving globally. He lives in Lima, Peru, with his wife, Shannon

title_zh: IMB传教士通过新信徒和当地教会看到神在工作
content: In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. IMB missionaries work alongside local believers and churches to fulfill the Great Commission. IMB Photo Twenty minutes had passed already. The sun was going down, and they were looking everywhere, but they only saw men in the park. Sophia, an International Mission Board missionary, joined another IMB missionary and Maryam, a South Asian Christian. They went to the park to share the gospel, but approaching a man in their Muslim-majority city was out of the question. They kept walking and watching. Even if they went home without a single conversation, Sophia knew Maryam would want to try again. This woman who had grown up with a distrust of Muslims, now searched a park for a Muslim woman to tell about Jesus. When Sophia first invited her along, Maryam never imagined a Muslim could come to know Jesus. But the more they went out sharing the gospel together, the more God softened her heart. “One day, I found she was sharing in the park by herself, without me,” Sophia said with a laugh. These days, she shares regularly — with classmates, with rickshaw drivers, with women in the park, when she can find them. God transformed Maryam’s heart. He could transform this walk through the park, too. “So we stopped,” Sophia said, “and prayed, ‘God, give us just one woman to talk to.’” Then they spotted her — a girl sitting alone on a bench. Meeting the girl on the bench She looked like other conservative Muslim women in the area, covered in black except for her face. They approached casually, not wanting to frighten her. It was Eid al-Adha – “one of the biggest Muslim holidays here,” Sophia said. They greeted her and asked about her holiday plans. Her name was Tara, and she wasn’t intimidated at all. “You may think I’m a Muslim from the way I dress,” she said, “but actually in my heart, I have left Islam.” “I was a little shocked,” Sophia said, hearing such a bold statement from a stranger. Tara told them she was a university student at a conservative Islamic school, but she had grown disillusioned and discontent with the religion. “ I don’t believe in Islam anymore,” Tara said. Without knowledge of God, she had no one to pray to, and it left her lonely. She’d been searching — Buddhism and Hinduism from friends, even a meeting with atheists, who struck her as unhappy, following only themselves. “Do you know any Christians?” Sophia asked. “Would you like to hear what we believe?” “Sure, please share.” They read about Jesus’ birth, and Tara was hungry for more. When she asked about church, Sophia described their congregation of about 40 believers, many from a Muslim background. Though she wasn’t ready to visit the church, Tara continued her interest in learning. Sophia and Maryam met with her every week in coffee shops, tea shops, Sophia’s home, wherever they could talkthat wasn’t too loud or have “too many ears and eyes” observing them. Finding her closest friend They read through the Gospel of John. One November day in a coffee shop, they reached the passage on the Samaritan woman at the well, and Sophia noticed Tara was crying. “Tara, I see you have tears,” Sophia said. “Let’s stop. Let’s talk about it .” That day, Tara prayed to receive Christ. Soon after, she wanted to visit the church, though nervous how believers would receive her in a hijab. “They will love you,” Sophia told her. “Don’t worry.” Tara went and was welcomed. That Christmas, 80 people packed Sophia’s apartment, singing and dancing in circles. Across the room, Sophia saw Tara, wearing red Christmas garland like a scarf and a smile stretched across her face. “Tara grew up very conservative – music was not even allowed in her home. But now she’s dancing, worshiping the Lord with us with music and songs.” In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. IMB missionaries work alongside local believers and churches to fulfill the Great Commission. IMB Photo That spring, Tara was baptized.

" Tara长大后非常保守——她家甚至不允许音乐. 现在她正在跳舞,用音乐和歌曲与我们一起崇拜上帝。 在南亚,玛丽安和一位当地牧师为新信徒塔拉施洗. IMB的传教士与当地的信徒和教会一起工作,完成"大委员会". IMB 相片 当年春天,塔拉被洗礼.

title_zh: 神通过IMB在意大利的传教士保持忠诚
content: The eastern face of St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican City in Rome, Italy, is famous for its central balcony from which popes give their papal addresses. Most people in Rome have at least a cultural connection to Roman Catholicism as the city is “the heart of Catholicism.” IMB Photo In the city where Jason and Lizzy Davis serve, some steps have a lot of meaning. And the meaning is different for them than it is for the thousands who travel there to visit that site. “If you come to Rome, you can come to a place called the Holy Steps,” Jason said. “People go there, and they’ll crawl up on their knees and pray the rosary all the way up.” From the top of the steps, a mural depicting Jesus on the Cross looks down on those making the pilgrimage. For Jason and Lizzy, it’s a spiritual experience, a picture of a religion that asks people to earn their way to Jesus. “That’s really the opposite of what the gospel is. The gospel is Jesus saying, ‘No, you can’t do it . . . no matter how good you think you are,’” they said. Most people in Rome have at the very least a cultural connection to Roman Catholicism, as the city is “the heart of Catholicism.” Jason explained, “It’s where the Pope lives in the Vatican. It’s very much part of the religion and culture. It’s all intertwined here.” An ‘unavoidable’ call Jason and Lizzy are investing their lives as International Mission Board missionaries in Rome, Italy, to share the truth of the gospel. The Davises partner with national believers through a new church plant, and they’re seeking to plant more churches within the city. Lizzy said for her, the call to missions was unavoidable. “I grew up as a third culture kid, or a missionary kid. My parents were on the mission field, as were my grandparents, all with the International Mission Board.” Then her family moved to Virginia for her dad to work for IMB’s home office staff. As a middle schooler and high schooler, every time Lizzy heard about the need for the gospel to go forth, she felt a burden, a “burning” in her heart. She didn’t know what God would do with that, but she had a feeling she would see one day. Now, years later, she and Jason spend their time trying to find as many opportunities as they can to invite people into their home so they can share the hope of Jesus with them. That can mean Bible study or simply sharing a meal. ‘Completely lost’ Jason has been surprised by just how often people are willing to talk about faith. “You can get into spiritual conversations very quickly with people, especially if you’re just open and honest with them.” Lizzy shared that one of the easiest ways to do this is to be willing to let your day be interrupted. “That’s something I’ve seen Jason do firsthand in our neighborhood. He walks down the street, and everybody knows him because he stops and takes the time to ask them questions about their families, gets to know people, gets to know the newspaper stand guy and the guy at the fruit stand and the grocery store ladies.” She emphasized that caring about people is “what Christ would do.” The Davises, whose previous mission service prevents their photos from being published, live in a neighborhood of about 130,000 people. Their church of 15 people is the only evangelical congregation there. Lizzy said the area is “truly a lost, completely lost, dark neighborhood” with people who have never heard the gospel. Thousands more come to their area on a religious quest. The Davis family’s neighborhood is home to the Basilica Papale di San Paolo (the Papal Basilica of Saint Paul), one of the city’s four major basilicas. “So we get a lot of people coming on spiritual journeys, visiting our neighborhood, seeking some sort of spiritual experience. And oftentimes it’s just trying to earn their salvation,” she added. Jason described this environment as “a genuine need for people to actually hear the gospel and know that their sins can be forgiven and they can have an assurance of that.” IMB missionaries Jason and Liz

title: Global missionary partners expand gospel work through IMB teams
summary: Rebeca Couto moved from one volcanic archipelago to another, leaving Portugal’s Azores islands to anchor her life in Japan. content: Rebeca Couto, a global missionary partner from the Azores islands, practices writing characters with her tutor in Japan. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto poses with her violin. Couto is a professional violinist who is serving as a global missionary partner with the IMB in Japan. Doors have opened for her to use her skills with evangel ical Japanese musicians who perform. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto moved from one volcanic archipelago to another, leaving Portugal’s Azores islands to anchor her life in Japan. The percentage of evangelical Christians in the Azores and Japan is similar, with both populations under 1%. Couto is a fourth-generation Christian, a rarity on the small islands. She is one of few, if any, believers in the Azores with such a long spiritual lineage. This rich legacy shaped her and prepared her for ministry. “I’ve always understood the Great Commission as a call for all believers and all disciples of Christ to be missionaries, wherever they are, whatever they’re doing, and whatever God has equipped them with,” Couto said. Couto’s great-grandfather became a Christian through the witness of missionaries from the United Kingdom. Later, missionaries from the Foreign Mission Board, now the International Mission Board, started the first Baptist work in the Azores by planting an English-speaking church near an American military base. A Baptist Brazilian couple planted a Portuguese-speaking church, which became the congregation where Couto grew up and was commissioned as a missionary. Ministry has been passed down through the generations of her family. Couto’s father has pastored for 20 years, and both of her parents have been involved in ministry for most of their lives. Couto now serves in Japan as a global missionary partner, a missionary who is financially supported by a sending church or organization in their home country and serves with IMB teams. Close to 400 GMPs currently serve on IMB teams around the world. Language learning Couto is immersed in language study in Yokohama, Japan. She had a head start before she even arrived. After graduating from high school, Couto moved from the Azores to Lisbon to pursue a degree in music. She spent hours on public transportation and wanted a challenge to pass the time. She decided to study Japanese because she thought it sounded beautiful. At the time, she had no intention of becoming a missionary in the traditional sense. However, the more she learned about the language and the culture, her burden for the lost grew. She began researching Christianity in Japan. “I understood how bleak the scenario was, and how much the country needed Jesus. I struggled with that calling because the doors were closed, and it didn’t seem possible to come to Japan for a myriad of reasons,” Couto said. After finishing master’s degrees in music and violin performance, along with a seminary degree, Couto was considering pursuing a Ph.D. or returning to seminary when her seminary professors, IMB missionaries Jonathan and Bethany Sharp, contacted her about serving as a missionary in Japan. They introduced her to the GMP program and invited her to attend a missions immersion school they piloted . Music to their ears As a professional violinist, Couto brought her violin to Japan, unsure of what opportunities existed, but she knew her call to the mission field somehow involved her gifting. “I see myself as having been called to serve through music. I never even conceived doing missions while excluding the violin entirely,” Couto said. She continued, “Music is such a universal way to connect with people, and it’s so intuitive to pair that with the gospel and with God’s message to people’s hearts.” While she knew the Lord would somehow open a door for her to use the violin for kingdom work, she was at peace with the possibility that, for a season, she may not be as active in music. That, however, was not the case. “I’ve always understood the Great Commission as a call for all believers and all disciples of Christ

title_zh: IMB传教士使用家庭、咖啡馆、应用程序为西班牙的福音对话敞开大门
content: Men and women gather to discuss spiritual topics with Caleb and Carina Beaty, International Mission Board missionaries who serve in Madrid. IMB Photo Across Spain, people looking for connection and meaningful conversation turn to the internet to find groups where they can meet others. At a café by the river, Caleb and Carina Beaty engage in conversations about finding purpose, beauty and “what’s wrong with the world.” A website called Meetup allows people to search for groups to meet in person. The description of the Beatys’ group indicates that it discusses spiritual topics. People come expecting to talk about faith, so it’s not a surprise when they arrive. Caleb said he always has a list of questions that begin broadly and funnel into questions such as, “If there were a God …” or “What do you think Christians believe about that?” or “Why do you think religions have such different perspectives?” The Beatys’ goal in these conversations is to work toward deeper worldview questions within 45 minutes to an hour. Most of the people who attend their Meetup group are from Madrid, but they also have conversations with people from other countries. During one Meetup, Caleb and Carina shared how creation was perfect, but sin led to a world separated from the Father. God offers salvation through the death and resurrection of Jesus, they explained. “There are times we’re able to get to a clear gospel presentation with a group of people, and sometimes we’re doing pre-evangelism.” Caleb said. Some repeat attendees who have been attending for more than a year quickly jump to the heart of the discussion. “All right, Caleb, what’s the Bible say about suffering?” they’ll ask. Caleb and Carina then have the opportunity to share the Christian perspective. IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty and their children pose for a photo in a park in Madrid, Spain.  IMB Photo Spain has secularized rapidly since the 1990s, Caleb said. While many may think of it as a Catholic nation, many people do not know the basic tenets of Christianity. “We’ve got all the churches, we’ve got the cathedrals, and they do processions, but the average person on the street does not know anything about the gospel and does not know anything about Jesus,” Caleb said. Younger Spaniards are drawn to their group and are receptive to the gospel because they don’t have a spiritual foundation or know anyone who does. “There’s just this curiosity because, for a lot of them, they’ve never met someone who actually believes that God exists, and that changes your life,” Carina said. “I’ve had people completely shocked that we believe in God. ‘You really believe that God exists?’ They can’t wrap their mind around that.” During one Meetup, a man contrasted Protestant and Catholic beliefs by saying Protestants focus on Jesus’ suffering and Catholics on Mary’s grief. Caleb responded that evangelicals focus on the resurrection. When Caleb said Jesus rose from the dead, the man replied that he needed to look into that. Caleb said encounters like that reveal how little many Spaniards know about the gospel. Caleb noted the irony of the man’s sharing the Catholic perspective without truly understanding it. He is not the only person the Beatys have met who has missed the heart of the gospel. A friend of the Beatys told them she’d heard Jesus died, but she hadn’t heard he rose from the dead. A man reads a passage of Scripture during a Bible study hosted by IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty at their family’s apartment in Madrid, Spain. Five atheists began attending their Bible study after attending the couple’s Meetup group. IMB Photo The Beatys also host seasonal outreach events through the Meetup. Members from their church in Madrid have started attending the Meetup to learn how the Beatys lead discussions. Their group has become so popular, a waitlist has formed. Caleb and Carina host a small-group Bible study in their home. Five atheists who joined their Meetup now attend the Bible study.

content: IMB Graphic NASHVILLE – As the books closed on the latest fiscal year, receipts for the two Southern Baptist national annual missions offerings underscored the value Southern Baptist churches place on reaching the world with the gospel. The Lottie Moon Christmas Offering® (LMCO) totaled $212.5 million to support International Mission Board (IMB) missionaries, and the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering® (AAEO) reached $73.6 million to support the North American Mission Board’s (NAMB) church planting, compassion ministry and other evangelistic efforts to reach North America. IMB President Paul Chitwood said he celebrates what God did in the 2025-26 season and what He is doing now to lead Southern Baptists toward historic generosity. “I thank God for Southern Baptists! With giving through the Lottie Moon offering at an all-time high, churches and individual givers continue to display a heart for the gospel to be proclaimed to every nation, all tribes, peoples and languages,” Chitwood said. The Annie total marked the second highest in NAMB’s history. The record Lottie Moon offering total surpassed last year’s total by more than $5 million and is the best offering in IMB history. “God is giving our generation unprecedented opportunity to send missionaries to the most unreached peoples and places,” Chitwood continued. “Though the challenges faced by our missionaries are enormous, the generosity of Southern Baptists ensures they have what they need to face those challenges and continue in the work while we hold the ropes with our support.” IMB missionary Landon Williams (center) walks with a Chilean pastor and a U.S. pastor on a remote island in Chile. Cooperation and generosity among Southern Baptists fuels the work to reach the uttermost parts of the world with the gospel. IMB Photo National goals for both offerings are set in partnership with Woman’s Missionary Union (WMU) each year. In response to the offering totals, Sandy Wisdom-Martin, executive director-treasurer of WMU, said: “As Southern Baptists, we are all in for His mission. When we give sacrificially, we prioritize the mission of God. Together our fervent prayers, our faithful generosity and our wholehearted obedience become channels for the gospel to reach our neighbors as well as the nations.” For the last 10 years, Southern Baptists have increasingly supported the Annie offering, setting records in seven of the last 10 years. Totals in each of the last four years have surpassed $70 million. “I am so grateful to the pastors and churches for the faithfulness and generosity they have demonstrated through this offering,” said NAMB president Kevin Ezell. “As I travel and speak in churches of all sizes, I love seeing the posters in the hallways showing their offering goals. For some it is a few hundred dollars, for others several thousand.” The Annie Armstrong offering supports more than 3,000 missionaries in North America, including the ongoing work of church planting in the U.S. and Canada. In 2025, Southern Baptists planted the largest number of churches, 699, since 2016. Including church plants and replants, Southern Baptists have surpassed 700 new churches in four of the last five years. More than 12,000 churches have been planted since 2010. The five consecutive years of increase marked the first such streak in approximately 75 years. title_zh: 俄克拉荷马州浸信会加入派遣教会实验室，以加强传教士支持
content: Staff members at First Baptist Church in Wagoner, Oklahoma, evaluate their church’s involvement with missions and missionary support. IMB Photo The chapel at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City turned into a science lab on Oct. 5-6. Microscopes, beakers and test tubes weren’t in the room, but this Sending Church Lab drew nearly 40 people representing 12 Oklahoma Baptist churches committed to send and care for international missionaries well. The Sending Church Lab, facilitated by the International Mission Board, brought pastors, church leaders and missionaries together for two days of discussion, self-assessment and planning centered on one question: What does it mean for a church to truly be a sending church? For Mike Wall, a global missions ministry partner of Oklahoma Baptists, the answer begins with churches reclaiming responsibility for the Great Commission. Wall first attended a Sending Church Lab last year in Tulsa with few expectations. He left convinced more churches needed the training. “When I went there, I thought, ‘You’ve got to do this in Oklahoma City,’” Wall said, “because of the content and how much our churches need something just like this.” After observing churches work through the exercises in the lab, Wall said he was encouraged by an emphasis on local church ownership in missions. “We can’t just send our people and say, ‘OK, now this is your job, IMB,’” he said. “We have to do our job in sending, preparing and training the best ‘sent ones’ so that when they get to the field, they can already hit the ground running.” Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement specialist, leads a Sending Church Lab at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City. He is emphasizing the importance of sending churches assessing and equipping future IMB missionaries. IMB Photo Leading the lab was Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement strategist, who developed the concept after seeing the need for stronger relationships between missionaries and local churches. “A Sending Church Lab is our attempt to raise up a host of IMB sending churches,” Wooten said, crediting the North American Mission Board for doing similar events and having successful results. The lab helps churches understand what Wooten calls the church engagement pathway: praying, cooperating, partnering and sending. While many churches faithfully pray, give and go, he said sending requires something more intentional. “Sending includes taking responsibility for an IMB missionary by providing ongoing encouragement, accountability and soul care throughout their term of service,” he explained. During the two-day event, participants gathered around whiteboards to evaluate their church’s missions practices, identify strengths and weaknesses and develop plans for improvement. “We don’t just need to deliver content,” Wooten said. “We need to invite churches to do some work on their own.” Rather than simply listening to presentations, attendees worked through practical questions about prayer, giving, short-term missions, missionary assessment and long-term care. Wooten said churches consistently tell him the greatest benefit is clarity. “They are thankful for clarity on what an IMB sending church is and what our roles and responsibilities are,” he said. For IMB missionaries Peter and Katie Weeks, that clarity is especially valuable. They participated in the lab alongside church leaders. Their real names have been changed to protect their work in Southeast Asia. “There’s no other place I’d rather be during these few days than here,” Peter said. Katie appreciated the interactive nature of the training. “I really appreciate the way they’re actually requiring information from the different churches and encouraging dialogue about how they can go through the steps,” she said. From a missionary perspective, she believes the lab addresses a common challenge. “It’s hard to know sometimes as churches how to be a good sending church and how to support missionaries,” she sa
content_zh: 俄克拉何马州瓦戈纳第一浸信会的工作人员评价了教会参与传教和传教活动的情况。 IMB 相片 俄克拉荷马城Constitute Road Baptist Church的小教堂于10月5-6日变成科学实验室. 但这个送信教会实验室吸引了近40人, 代表12个俄克拉何马浸会教会, 传教士实验室在国际传教委员会的协助下,召集牧师、教会领袖和传教士进行两天的讨论、自我评估和规划,其中心是一个问题: 教会真正成为送教之所意味着什么? 对于俄克拉何马浸信会的全球使命部合作伙伴迈克·沃尔来说,答案始于教会重新为大委员会负责。 去年沃尔在图尔萨参加了一个送教实验室, 他离开后确信更多的教会需要训练. “当我去那里时,我想,`你必须在俄克拉荷马城做这件事,'墙说,`因为内容和我们的教会需要这样的东西。 在观察了教堂通过实验室的演练工作后,沃尔说,他在任务中强调当地教会的所有权使他受到鼓舞. “我们不能只是派我们的人来说,“好吧,这是你的工作,IMB。” “我们必须在派遣、准备和训练最优秀的`派遣 ' 人员方面完成我们的工作,这样,当他们到达实地时,他们就已经可以奔跑地了。” Bryan Wooten,IMB高级教会订婚专家,在俄克拉荷马城的Constitution Road Baptist教堂领导一个送教实验室. 他强调派遣教会评估和装备未来的IMB传教士的重要性. IMB Photo Leading the lab是IMB高级教会接触策略师布莱恩·伍滕(Bryan Wooten),他在看到传教士与本地教会之间需要更牢固的关系后发展出这个概念. 伍腾说,“一个派遣教会实验室是我们努力培养许多派遣教会的IMB。 ”他赞扬北美传教委员会开展了类似的活动并取得了成功。 实验室帮助教会理解伍腾所谓的教会参与途径:祈祷,合作,合作和发送. 虽然许多教堂忠实地祈祷,奉献和去,但他说送去需要更有意图的东西. 他解释说,“最后包括负责一个IMB传教士,在整个任职期间提供持续的鼓励、问责和精神关怀。” 在为期两天的活动期间,与会者聚集在白板周围,评价其教会的任务做法,查明优缺点并制订改进计划。 」伍腾说: “我们需要邀请教会自己做一些工作。” 与会者不是简单地听取演讲,而是通过祷告、赠送、短期访问、传教士评估和长期照料等实际问题开展工作。 Wooten说,教会总是告诉他最大的好处是清晰. 他说,“他们感谢对派遣教会的咨监委的澄清,以及我们的作用和责任。” 对于IMB的传教士彼得和凯蒂·威克斯来说,这种清晰度特别有价值. 他们与教会领袖一起参加了实验室. 他们的真名被更改以保护自己在东南亚的工作. 彼得说,“在这几天里,我宁愿呆在这里。” 凯蒂对培训的互动性表示赞赏. 我非常欣赏他们要求不同教会提供信息的方式, 从传教士的角度来看,她认为实验室解决了共同的挑战. title_zh: 神圣的盛宴让饕餮之徒望洋兴叹
content: It’s feasting season. Thanksgiving. Advent. New Year’s. But for Americans in particular, is there such a thing as a non -feasting season? Our society has a bizarre love-hate relationship with food, pulling the plate toward us with one hand while pushing it away with the other. On the one hand, about 40 percent of adults are clinically obese; on the other, more than one in eight adults rely on GLP-1 to suppress their appetite. We want food and we want to want food less. We struggle to break free from the clutches of Big Food, so we look to Big Pharma for help. Happy Thanksgiving? What’s the remedy for this gastronomic schizophrenia? As counterintuitive as it sounds, godly feasting provides an antidote to foolish gluttony. Feasting vs. Feeding The Bible has a lot to say about food, not just in isolated verses but in plot points central to the arc of Scripture. Many of the most egregious sins centered on food. For instance, the first sin involved rebellious eating, looking to something forbidden in search of goodness (Genesis 3:6). After the exodus, Israel grumbled about their desire for Pharaoh’s pots of meat (Exodus 16:3). Then, when the Lord provided manna in the wilderness, Israel reenacted the sin of Eve when they gathered food on the Sabbath against God’s command (Exodus 16:27–30). But the Bible also commends feasting, both spiritual and physical. Jesus offers himself as the bread of life, given for the nourishment of the saints in exile (John 6:35). And the church looks forward to a meal at the consummation of history, the marriage feast of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Between the resurrection and return of the Lamb, we weekly feast on his body and blood, anchoring our minds on what Christ has done and what Christ will do (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). Godly feasting leans into our place in between the times by remembering with gratitude what was and anticipating with joy what will be. All the blessed feasts in the Scriptures are communal celebrations . Something extraordinary has happened; raise a glass to the King! We shouldn’t eat what we regularly eat today; instead, “bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found!” (Luke 15:23–24). We break from feeding ourselves (simply giving our body what it needs) in order to feast (eating and drinking more than we need) as a blessed means of joyously celebrating the work of God in history. But most Christians rarely, if ever, truly feast with mindful gratitude. We just overeat. Spiritual Malnutrition “A companion of gluttons shames his father” (Proverbs 28:7). The glutton does not feast; his god is his belly. He looks for deliverance in his next snack, his next meal, his next drink. He does not fully grasp that man does not live by bread alone. He is not marked by gratitude. The emptiness in his soul, the purposelessness of his life, and the joylessness of his ease have taken root as a spiritual disease. “A glutton is one who raids the icebox for a cure for spiritual malnutrition,” Frederick Buechner observed ( Wishful Thinking , 35). Americans, overall, remain locked in a permanent state of pseudo-feasting. Our culture combines industrial-grade, highly addictive food products and dopamine-seeking, nihilistic joylessness. We mindlessly munch. Often, we hardly even taste or enjoy our food. (A 2026 JAMA study revealed 69 percent of kids and 78 percent of adults use screens while eating.) This is an often-undiscussed problem within the church. I don’t know any Christians who intend to be gluttonous. But I know many, myself included, who have at times felt buried by the shame that follows an episode or season marked by a lack of self-control. We know we cannot make peace with sin, but we aren’t sure what this specific path of repentance looks like. So, when believers recognize the shameful pattern, we try to restrict our calories or go on a diet, which doesn’t stick. We purge and we binge — godless,

content: “Hold the lettuce.” The simple sentence, perhaps stated more frequently than we might hope, captures a crucial hallmark that predominates in the thinking of many. At a recent lunch with a friend, I saw this firsthand. For my friend, it wasn’t just the lettuce. The instructions he gave restrained the cook from adding anything remotely vegetable-like to the hamburger. Notwithstanding my jibe, my friend held fast to his decision. He was the one ordering. And he expected (rightly so!) to be served what he desired. After all, the customer is king. This cluster of expectations animates the modern marketplace. We want products tailored to our specific needs. We seek out services that let us pay only for what we want. We get frustrated when we take the car to a mechanic who not only fixes the problem we knew about but also takes the liberty of repairing other problems (and charging liberally for them). In short, we want (and expect) to be served according to our preferences and felt needs. Innocuous enough when it comes to the morsels on our plates, the reign of personal preferences involves more serious implications when it extends over the rest of life. And in the life of faith, the consequences are serious indeed. For preference-driven faith will, in the end, produce a Christless Christianity. Have It Your Way What do we hope for when we join the church for worship? Parsing motives presents no easy project, especially if there are children in tow or responsibilities for some aspect of the service or fellowship. Few of us have the personal or cognitive space to search out the depths of our hearts en route to the Sunday morning service. But the way home often presents opportunities to interrogate those hidden recesses. The questions we pose shed light on what is in our hearts: “How did you like the sermon this morning?” “Didn’t the worship team nail it today?” We tend to ask not about a confrontation with gospel truth but about measures of personal satisfaction. If our questions begin illuminating this tendency, the answers we give put our motives on clear display: “I thought the pastor did a great job! I really liked . . .” or “Ya know, I just wasn’t feeling it this morning; the sermon didn’t really speak to me.” “Yes, the worship was great!” or “I thought the team was a bit off. Did you hear them mess up on that one song?” So often, whether at the sandwich shop or on the way home from church, preference-driven language bubbles out of our mouths like boiling water from an unwatched pot. For many, our post-service concerns center far too frequently on how well certain aspects of the service met our felt needs. What did I gain from the sermon? Did I enjoy the music? Service to the ascendant self predominates. We reflect on the worship gathering in a manner unsettlingly similar to how we might reflect on a hamburger: It was decent, but I’ve had better elsewhere. I think they overdid the mayonnaise, and I would have preferred sesame rather than a brioche bun. Whether we want to admit it or not, our expectations of being served as we please spill into our perceived relationship to the church’s gathered worship. Those same expectations shape how we approach our Lord. We tend naturally, in our sin, to want merely an affirming savior. We like to hear that Jesus loves sinners so much that he died to win them, for hearing this affirms that our need for forgiveness has been met. We like to hear that his love for his sheep never falters, for hearing this quells the fear that perhaps our snide words or dubious choices or the train wreck of our inner thoughts might put our hope in jeopardy. We like to hear how our Lord railed against the hypocrisy and legalism of the Pharisees, for hearing this makes us smile inwardly, pleased that we are not so pretentious and uptight. Messages such as these leave us content, unruffled, ready to carry on with life as normal, affirmed in our preferred way of life by a (truncated) gospel that accomplishes little b
content_zh:
“抓住生菜。” 这个简单的句子,也许比我们所希望的更频繁地说,抓住了在许多人的思想中占主导地位的关键标志。 最近和一个朋友共进午餐时 我亲眼看到的 对我的朋友来说, 他给厨师的指示 禁止在汉堡里添加任何类似蔬菜的东西

我的朋友坚持他的决定 是他订的 他希望自己所欲达到的, 毕竟客为王. 这一组期望激发出现代市场。 我们需要适合我们具体需要的产品。 我们寻求服务,让我们只为所欲为。

我们感到沮丧的是,我们把车送到一个技工那里,他不仅解决了我们所知道的问题,而且还自由地修复了其他问题(并且对这些问题收取宽松的费用)。 简言之,我们希望(并期望)根据我们的喜好和感受到的需要得到服务。

谈到我们盘子里的泥潭时,个人偏好的统治,如果延续到余生,就会产生更严重的影响。 在信仰的生活中,后果确实很严重。 因为受偏好驱使的信仰,最终会产生出一种没有基督的基督教. 我们加入教堂做礼拜时希望什么?

分析动机并非易事,特别是如果有儿童被拖走或承担某些方面的服务或研究金责任。 我们当中很少有人拥有个人或认知空间,在前往周日早间礼拜的路上去探寻内心深处. 但回家的方式往往为审讯那些隐蔽的休庭提供了机会。

我们提出的问题揭示了我们心中的心事,“你今天早上喜欢讲道吗?” 我们往往不问与福音真相的对抗,而是问个人满意的措施。 如果我们的问题开始说明这一趋势,我们给出的答案清楚地显示了我们的动机:“我认为牧师做了一件伟大的工作!

我真的很喜欢. . . . . . . . . “是的,崇拜是伟大的!”或“我认为队伍有点偏差。 你听到他们把那首歌弄乱了吗?” 所以,无论是在三明治店,还是在从教堂回家的路上,偏好驱动的语言泡从我们嘴里喷出,就像从一个无人观察的锅中取出沸水来.

对许多人来说,我们的服务后关切过于频繁地集中在服务的某些方面在多大程度上满足了我们的需要。 我从布道中得到什么? 我很喜欢音乐吗? 服务于上层的自我占主导地位。 我们以令人不安的方式思考礼拜聚会, 但我在别处生活得更好。

我觉得他们做了蛋黄酱, 我更喜欢芝麻,而不是布洛克包。 无论我们是否愿意承认这一点,我们期望得到服务,因为我们希望与教会所聚集的礼拜的感同身受。 同样的期望决定了我们如何接近我们的主。 我们的罪孽中,自然而然地只想要一个坚定的救世主。

我们喜欢听到耶稣如此地爱罪人,以至于他为了赢得他们的胜利而去死,因为听到这个消息,肯定了我们对宽恕的需要已经得到满足了. 我们想听到,他对他的羊的爱从未动摇,因为听到这种平息的恐惧,也许我们的暗语或可疑的选择,或者我们内心思想的火车残骸会使我们的希望陷入危险.

我们想听听我们的主如何反对法利赛人的虚伪和法西斯主义,因为听到这使我们对内微笑,很高兴我们没有这么自大和紧张。 这样的讯息给我们留下了内容,没有磨损,准备继续正常生活,在我们所偏爱的生活方式中,用一个(经磨练的)福音来证实,这些福音成就不大。
